title: Valid Anagram
description: Check whether two strings are made of exactly the same characters, in any order.
statement:
Given two strings `a` and `b`, return `True` if `b` can be made by rearranging the characters of `a`, and `False` otherwise.

- Every character counts, including spaces, digits, punctuation and letters outside English. Capital letters are different from lowercase ones: `"Listen"` and `"silent"` are not anagrams.
- Two empty strings are anagrams. Strings of different lengths never are.

**Examples**

```python
is_anagram("anagram", "nagaram")   # True
is_anagram("rat", "car")           # False
is_anagram("aab", "abb")           # False: same letters, different counts
```

Aim for O(n) (O(n log n) is fine too): the last tests use strings of 120,000 characters.
tests: accented, rearranged = "caf\u00e9", "\u00e9fac"   # the same four letters; escapes keep this test code plain ASCII
assert is_anagram("x" * 60_000 + "y" * 60_000, "y" * 60_000 + "x" * 60_000) == True, "too slow or wrong on 120,000 characters"
assert is_anagram("x" * 60_000 + "y" * 60_000, "y" * 60_000 + "x" * 59_999 + "z") == False, "too slow or wrong on 120,000 characters"
hints: Two strings are anagrams exactly when every character occurs the same number of times in both. How could you find out how many times each character occurs?
Count the characters of each string (a dictionary, or `collections.Counter`) and compare the two counts. Comparing the lengths first is a cheap early exit.
Comparing only which letters appear is not enough (`"aab"` and `"abb"`), and neither is comparing the sum of the character codes (`"ad"` and `"bc"`).
explanation:
**The idea.** Two strings are anagrams exactly when every character occurs the same number of times in both. `Counter` builds those counts in one pass, and comparing two counters is a dictionary comparison. Checking the lengths first rejects most non-anagrams without counting anything.

**Why not compare the sets of letters?** `"aab"` and `"abb"` use the same letters with different counts. Comparing the sum of the character codes fails as well: `"ad"` and `"bc"` have the same sum.

**Complexity.** O(n) time and O(k) space for k different characters. `sorted(a) == sorted(b)` is also correct and shorter, at O(n log n). If the input were only `a`-`z`, a fixed list of 26 counters would be faster and use constant space.

**Follow-up.** With Unicode text, `"é"` can be one character or an `e` followed by an accent mark. Normalise both strings first (`unicodedata.normalize("NFC", s)`) if you want those to match.
